newsitem.title: UK: UK plans "revolution" in pensions provision.
newsitem.headline: UK plans "revolution" in pensions provision.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Wednesday proposed a "revolution" in Britain's pension system aimed at easing the burden on future taxpayers and requiring people to take more responsibility for their own affairs.
The plan seeks to defuse a pensions bombshell that could go off next century, when an ageing population will have to be supported by a shrinking workforce.
Major said Britain had already put aside more to provide for future pension liabilities than the rest of the European Union combined.
"This will put us another huge step ahead -- enabling us to sustain a healthy, low-tax economy for the future," he told a news conference at his Downing Street residence.

Major's Conservative government is searching for big issues that would help them to claw back the main opposition Labour party's big lead in opinion polls of 15-20 percentage points in the run-up to a general election expected on May 1.
But with the pension reforms due to be phased in over a generation, Major said it was wrong to portray them as designed to win votes.
If the Conservatives win a fifth consecutive term of office, they will consult widely on the proposals before legislating towards the end of the next five-year parliament, Major said.
Under Major's complex proposals, every individual would build up a personal savings and investment fund in their own name that would provide an income on retirement.
To feed the account, employees would be given a rebate on part of their national insurance conributions -- a payroll tax used to fund pensions and welfare benefits.

The state would thus no longer have to finance basic pensions, as now, from tax revenues. This would save the government an estimated 40 billion pounds a year by the middle of next century, Major said.

Employees would choose which company they wanted to manage their money. Given reasonable investment growth, the fund should yield a pension that is considerably greater than the current basic state pension.
But Major said the state would underwrite the scheme and guarantee that everyone received their basic pension entitlement, indexed as now to the rate of inflation.
The prime minister said the reform was in the best traditions of the ruling Conservative party's philosophy.

"It is dealing with the long-term issues in a far-sighted way. It is reinforcing the security and independence of individuals and families by building up their own assets and resources. It will provide funds for investment in the economy.
"It is prudent with public finances. And it safeguards people's expectations," Major said.

The government was embarrassed when its attempts to move people into private pensions went badly wrong in the late 1980s, with many people who had been sold the wrong pension plans having to be compensated.
Another aspect of the reforms would lead to the phasing-out of the state earnings-related pension scheme (SERPS), which provides about 6.5 million people with a second pension.
Harriet Harman, Labour's social security spokeswoman, said Labour would look carefully at the proposals.
"But at first sight they present a chilling prospect for hard-working families. The proposals mean the end of state pensions," Harman said in a statement.
